slides.title: Who can do what, everywhere
points: Identity and access management (IAM) decides which people and services can use which systems and data.
Most breaches involve stolen or misused credentials, so this is the front door.

slides.title: Authenticate strongly, authorise narrowly
points: Single sign-on gives one strong identity per person, with multi-factor authentication (passkeys or app-based codes, not SMS where avoidable).
Roles and groups grant access; nobody gets permissions one at a time by hand.
Least privilege and just-in-time elevation keep standing access small.
Joiner, mover, leaver: access changes the day someone's role changes or they leave.

slides.title: Friction against risk
points: Strong authentication adds steps; phishing-resistant methods (passkeys) add little friction.
Shared accounts are convenient and make every action anonymous.
Service accounts outnumber people and are often the weakest; give them owners.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Quarterly access reviews by each system's owner.
Alerts on new admin grants and on sign-ins from unusual places.
Break-glass accounts locked away, monitored and tested.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Noticing an attack in progress
points: Prevention eventually fails; detection finds attackers before they finish.
It depends on collecting the right logs and turning them into alerts people act on.

slides.title: Collect, correlate, alert
points: Collect security-relevant logs: sign-ins, admin actions, cloud API calls, network flows, endpoint events.
Send them to a central store (a SIEM) where they're kept, searched and correlated.
Detections are rules or models for suspicious patterns: impossible travel, mass downloads, new admin users.
Every alert needs a response plan; unreviewed alerts are noise.

slides.title: Coverage against noise and cost
points: Logging everything is expensive; prioritise what attackers touch.
Too many low-quality alerts bury the real one; tune continuously.
Attackers delete local logs, so ship them off the machine quickly.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Detections mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques to find gaps.
Log retention long enough to investigate an intrusion found months later.
Regular tests: simulate an attack and check it's detected.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Attacking your own systems, with permission
points: A penetration test is an authorised, scoped attempt to break into systems, to find weaknesses before real attackers do.
Written permission and a clear scope come before any testing.

slides.title: Recon, exploit, report
points: Reconnaissance: map what's exposed (hosts, ports, apps, people).
Find and confirm vulnerabilities; exploit carefully to show real impact without damage.
Pivot: from one foothold, see what else is reachable.
Report: each finding with evidence, risk, and a fix, written for the people who must fix it.

slides.title: Snapshot, not guarantee
points: A test covers a scope at a moment; new code brings new bugs.
Automated scanners are broad and shallow; manual testing is narrow and deep.
Testing production finds real issues and risks real disruption; agree the rules first.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Rules of engagement signed before starting.
Burp Suite, nmap and common tools, used only within scope.
Retests to confirm fixes.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Practising attack and defence together
points: A red team simulates a real adversary against the organisation; a blue team defends and detects.
Purple teaming puts them side by side to improve detection quickly.

slides.title: Goals, not just bugs
points: Red teams pursue an objective (reach the customer database) by any realistic path, often quietly over weeks.
Blue teams monitor, detect, respond and harden.
Exercises are measured by detection and response: how fast was it spotted, and contained?
Findings feed new detections and fixes.

slides.title: Realism against cost
points: Full red-team exercises are expensive and need mature defences to be worth it.
Secret exercises test real response but can cause alarm; leadership must know.
Purple exercises improve faster and test less realistically.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Attack paths described with MITRE ATT&CK.
Tabletop exercises for leadership.
Detection gaps tracked to closure.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Handling a breach
points: Security incident response contains an attack, removes the attacker, recovers systems and learns from it.
Forensics gathers evidence of what happened, carefully enough to rely on.

slides.title: Prepare, contain, eradicate, recover
points: Prepare: plans, contacts, logging and tools in place before anything happens.
Contain: isolate affected systems and disable compromised accounts, without destroying evidence.
Eradicate the attacker's access everywhere, then recover from known-good state.
Preserve evidence (disk and memory images, logs) with a record of who handled it.

slides.title: Speed against evidence
points: Wiping a machine stops the attacker there and destroys evidence of how far they got.
Acting before you know the full scope can tip off the attacker.
Legal and notification duties start early; involve legal and communications.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: An incident retainer with outside responders.
Playbooks for common cases: ransomware, account takeover, data leak.
Credentials reset broadly after a confirmed intrusion.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Security as a managed business risk
points: Governance decides which risks matter, who owns them and what's done about them.
Compliance frameworks (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, GDPR) set requirements customers and laws expect.

slides.title: Risks, controls, evidence
points: A risk register lists risks with likelihood, impact, owner and treatment.
Controls are the measures that reduce risk: access reviews, encryption, backups, training.
Audits check that controls exist and work, using evidence.
Policies say what must happen; procedures say how.

slides.title: Compliant isn't the same as secure
points: Passing an audit shows controls on paper; attackers test them in practice.
Too much process slows teams and pushes work around controls.
Automating evidence (from systems, not screenshots) makes audits cheaper and more honest.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Security questionnaires from customers before they buy.
Annual audits with continuous evidence collection.
Data protection duties: knowing what personal data you hold and why.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Find the risks in a design, live
points: You're shown a system (a file-sharing app, a payments flow) and asked what could go wrong and what you'd do about it.
They're scoring structure and prioritisation.

slides.title: A method out loud
points: Clarify the system and draw the data flow with trust boundaries.
Walk the boundaries with STRIDE or similar prompts.
Rank threats by impact and likelihood; don't list 40 equally.
Propose practical mitigations and say what you'd accept.

slides.title: Breadth against depth
points: Listing every possible threat runs out the clock; go deep on the top few.
Mitigations that break the product won't be adopted; balance them.
Say your assumptions; the interviewer may change them.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Practise on three common systems with a timer.
Know the usual mitigations for each STRIDE category.
Bring a real example from your own work.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: 'An alert fires; walk us through it'
points: Interviewers describe an incident (a suspicious login, ransomware on a laptop) and ask what you'd do step by step.
They're scoring calm, order, and knowing when to escalate.

slides.title: Triage to recovery
points: Triage: is it real, how severe, what's affected?
Contain with minimal evidence loss; escalate and involve the right people.
Investigate scope: other accounts, other machines, data accessed.
Recover, then improve detections and controls.

slides.title: Act fast, but in order
points: Overreacting (shutting down everything) has costs; underreacting lets it spread.
Communicating clearly to non-technical people is part of the job.
Say what evidence you'd look at and why.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Practise with common scenarios: phishing, credential theft, ransomware, data exfiltration.
Know a framework (NIST or SANS phases) to structure answers.
Have one real incident story ready.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Find the bugs in a snippet
points: You're given code (often a small web endpoint) and asked to find security issues and propose fixes.
They're checking that you can spot real vulnerabilities and explain them.

slides.title: Trace input to sinks
points: Identify untrusted inputs: parameters, headers, cookies, uploaded files.
Follow them to dangerous sinks: queries, shell commands, HTML output, file paths, redirects, deserialisation.
Check authentication and authorisation on every action.
Propose a specific fix and explain why it works.

slides.title: Real issues over style
points: Commenting on naming wastes time; focus on exploitable flaws.
Rank findings by severity.
Explain impact in plain words: what an attacker could actually do.

slides.title: How to prepare
points: Practise on deliberately vulnerable apps (OWASP Juice Shop, WebGoat).
Know the fix for each common class.
Read real security advisories for familiar libraries.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: An employee left three months ago, and their account still signed in yesterday. What process failed?
choices: Leaver deprovisioning: access should be removed the day someone leaves, ideally automatically from the HR system
Password rotation
Firewall rules
Backups
why: Offboarding must remove access promptly and completely.

newQuestions.stem: Investigating a breach, you find the attacker was inside for four months, but logs are only kept for 30 days. What should change?
choices: Keep security logs centrally for long enough to investigate slow intrusions (often a year), off the affected machines
Delete logs faster to save money
Log less
Rely on memory of the team
why: Long-dwell attacks need long retention to reconstruct.
Fewer logs means less to investigate with.

newQuestions.stem: You find a system outside the agreed scope that looks vulnerable during a test. What do you do?
choices: Stop, don't test it, and report it to the client to decide whether to add it to scope
Test it quickly since it's vulnerable
Ignore it entirely
Post about it publicly
why: Testing outside written scope is unauthorised access.
Being vulnerable doesn't make it authorised.

newQuestions.stem: After a red-team exercise, what's the most valuable output for the blue team?
choices: A timeline of the attack steps with what was and wasn't detected, turned into new detections and fixes
A score out of ten
A list of tools the red team used
A certificate
why: Detection gaps mapped to steps are directly actionable.
A score says little about what to fix.
Useful context, but not the main value.

newQuestions.stem: A server shows signs of compromise. A teammate wants to reinstall it immediately. What should happen first?
choices: Isolate it from the network and capture evidence (memory and disk image, logs) before rebuilding
Reinstall it right away
Leave it running normally to watch
Turn it off and throw it away
why: Isolation stops spread; evidence shows how they got in and what else they reached.
Loses evidence and doesn't find other compromised systems.

newQuestions.stem: A company passed its SOC 2 audit, then suffered a breach through an unpatched server. What does this show?
choices: Compliance shows controls exist on paper at audit time; security needs them to work continuously (patching, monitoring)
The audit was fake
SOC 2 prevents breaches
Servers can't be patched
why: Audits sample controls; they don't guarantee them.

newQuestions.stem: In a threat-modelling round you've listed 25 threats in 10 minutes. What's the better next move?
choices: Rank them and go deep on the top few: why they matter, how likely, and specific mitigations
List 25 more
Stop and wait for questions
Pick one at random
why: Prioritising shows judgement, which is what's being scored.

newQuestions.stem: Scenario: a user reports they entered their password on a fake login page an hour ago. What are your first steps?
choices: Reset their password and sessions, check sign-in logs for use of the account, and look for the same phishing email sent to others
Tell them to be more careful next time
Wait for suspicious activity
Wipe their laptop immediately
why: Contain the credential, check for misuse, and find other victims.
The attacker may already be in.
The laptop may not be involved at all.

newQuestions.stem: A snippet builds a SQL query with f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'". What do you say?
choices: SQL injection: user input becomes SQL; use a parameterised query with the name as a bound parameter
It's fine if the name is short
Escape quotes by hand
Use SELECT name instead of SELECT *
why: Parameters keep data separate from code.
Hand-escaping is easy to get wrong.
